title: Central Banking
content:
Norway’s central bank held its key interest rate, but kept open the possibility of further policy tightening should inflation remain high.

The conflict has lifted energy prices, though they have fallen since the midterms raised hopes for an end to the war.

Find insight on Swiss Re, Commerzbank and more in the latest Market Talks covering Financial Services.

The central bank expects Malaysia’s economy to grow more than 5% in 2026 and remain resilient in 2027.

Brazil’s central bank held its steep interest rates unchanged after five consecutive cuts as inflation drifted away from target amid growing concern around government spending.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh answered questions on the upcoming midterm elections and if they factored into the Fed's decision to keep interest rates at current levels. Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg News

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh answers questions about AI spending and the effect of rate hikes on financial markets. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh answered questions about the Fed not achieving price stability. Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh held a news conference following the central bank's decision to keep interest rates unchanged. Photo: Saul Loeb/Agence France-Presse/Getty Images

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to hold interest rates steady this week, although inflation data this month strengthened the case for raising them. WSJ’s chief economics correspondent breaks down what to expect. Photo Illustration: Noah Higgins-Dunn

The WSJ Dollar Index fell 0.3%, down five of the past six trading days.

The Institute for Supply Management’s purchasing managers index for services providers was 54.5 in October, compared with 54.9 in September. Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected a reading of 54.8.

The U.S. Treasury said Wednesday that it plans to keep long-term borrowing levels unchanged in coming months.

Gold prices extended gains, supported by a softer dollar and falling Treasury yields after the U.S. midterm election results.

Sweden’s central bank raised its key interest rate for the first time since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran, and signaled that more increases in borrowing costs were likely.

The unemployment rate rose to 5.7%, its highest level since mid-2015, defying expectations of a fall and affirming the central bank’s recent caution around raising interest rates further.

Macklem defended the decision to raise interest rates to 2.5% last week, saying officials needed to address a buildup of cost pressures and expectations that a larger share of firms would raise their prices over the next 12 months.

U.S. job openings rose in September while hiring held relatively steady, according to a report from the Labor Department’s monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey.

The institutions bought gold at the fastest pace since late 2024, as geopolitical risks and concerns over fiscal discipline bolstered demand, the World Gold Council said.

Annual inflation was 1.5% in October, compared with 1.0% in the prior month, Switzerland’s statistics office said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest since 2008 after “materially” revising up its inflation forecasts.

The People’s Bank of China said it would hike the foreign-exchange reserve requirement ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points to 6%.

Headline inflation eased in October but remained above the central bank’s 2% target.

The WSJ Dollar Index fell 0.1%, down for four consecutive trading days.

The Institute for Supply Management’s purchasing managers’ index was 55.5 in October – higher than the September figure of 54.5.

title: Consumers
content:
Voters head to the polls on Tuesday as beneficiaries of a stable job market and fatter salaries, but frustrated with the cost of living and President Trump’s handling of the economy.

The economy expanded 3.4% last quarter, driven by businesses and consumers and adding to evidence of an economy on a solid footing.

The country’s consumer-climate index fell to minus 30.8 in its forecast for November, from minus 30.6 in October.

The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index rose to 91.7 in October, above the 84.2 of September and economists’ expectations of a reading of 81.

Retail spending by Canadians looks to have remained on the rise last month, though the pace is showing signs of cooling as uncertainty and gasoline prices remain high.

As extended drought shrinks the river, a new federal plan threatens deep cuts for millions of people. We break down the century-old math failure behind the crisis—and what it would take to address it. Photo Illustration: Josh Lisanby

What is the state of the meatpacking industry in the midst of Americans’ protein craze? Wesley Batista Filho, JBS USA chief executive, reflects on his path to the top of his family’s company, and discusses the challenges facing cattle ranchers, farmers and consumers. Photo: Christopher Dilts for WSJ

In 2022, economic commentator Kyla Scanlon coined the phrase "vibesession" to describe the disconnect between positive economic data and poor consumer sentiment. She discusses the current state of the U.S. economy and the factors that shape consumer sentiment. Photo: Katelyn Tucker/Nikki Ritcher for WSJ

New research shows America’s upper-middle class is growing, while the country’s core middle class is shrinking. WSJ’s Rachel Louise Ensign explains the differences between the two groups. Photo Illustration: Ryan Trefes

A panel of executives offer a data-centric view of the economy, focusing on consumer health, labor market shifts, and the aggressive integration of AI within corporate structures. Photo: Nikki Ritcher for WSJ

The University of Michigan survey’s headline index came in at 48, down from 48.1 in September and hovering near record-low levels.

Consumer sentiment tumbled at the fastest pace since the Covid-19 pandemic this month as mounting cost-of-living pressures reversed the bounce in optimism seen over the summer.

Even as China makes strides in areas such as AI, much of its domestic economy is dragged down by gloomy consumer sentiment and a real-estate slump.

Has the economy gotten better or worse during President Trump’s second term? Food and gas prices are up, but so are 401(k) balances.

The hotter reading is a sign that high energy prices are tightening their squeeze on consumers ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Inflation is cooler than it was four years ago, but voters are still paying much higher prices.

Executives at America’s second-largest supermarket chain are in search of a turnaround as consumers spend less.

A Federal Reserve study found overall median net worth rose 2% between 2022 and 2025.

The University of Michigan survey’s headline index fell to 46.3 in its preliminary October reading, versus 48.1 in September.

Sales of food, drinks and non-fuel products rose slightly on the month in the 21-member currency area.

Spending is rising because prices are climbing and Americans are buying more stuff.

The U.S. economy grew more than previously thought in the second quarter of 2026 and inflation remained firm in August, according to new reports.

The research group said its consumer confidence index fell by 6.7 points to 81.9 following two prior months of softening.

Fewer new models are hitting the market than at any time in recent history—a hangover from the industry’s shift to EVs and its abrupt pullback.

The University of Michigan survey’s headline index landed at 48.1 in September, down from 51.7 in August.

title: Housing
content:
Zillow reported a decline in traffic to its apps and sites in the midst of what it called “one of the toughest housing markets in a generation.”

Real-estate giant Brookfield chose to give back the property rather than refinance its debt.

The Iran war, tariffs and the AI build-out have pushed up the costs of materials, labor and borrowing.

The YIGBY movement has churches building apartments on their property, easing shortages while sustaining their ministries.

The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller National Home Price Index, which measures home prices across the country, rose 2.1% in the 12 months through August, compared with a 1.9% increase in July.

WSJ’s Nicholas Miller explains in three charts whether 7% mortgage rates will become the new normal in the housing market. Photo: Laura Fong

Voters are frustrated by home prices, and the Senate will soon take up the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. But the bill is a 300-page melange of federal grants and pilot programs, plus a progressive ban on home purchases by big investors. Plus, 22 states sue over Donald Trump's tariffs under Section 122. Photo: Chris Arbisi

Journal Editorial Report: Will President Trump's proposals boost homeownership Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP/Mike Blake/Reuters

President Trump says he wants to ban "large institutional investors" from buying single-family homes, taking up another cause long championed by progressives. Is this more populist scapegoating?

Review & Outlook: Donald Trump seems to have bought Bill Pulte’s high-risk brainstorm that would benefit those in the home-building and mortgage-banking industries but squeeze borrowers at taxpayer expense. Photo: eduardo munoz/Reuters/Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Housing starts fell 5.2% in September to 1.221 million. Economists had expected a reading of 1.3 million and for starts to rise 2% over the month.

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, a gauge of builder confidence in the market for newly built single family housing, fell three points to 29 in October. That’s the lowest reading since June 2012.

Surging mortgage rates are sending many buyers to the sidelines, while affluent shoppers are driving overall prices higher with big cash purchases.

Canadian housing starts picked up last month though the pace remains soft as the broader market shows signs of cooling into the end of the year.

Home building, which relies on foreign-born workers, is suffering a labor shortage that is freezing projects and raising costs.

Plus, the developer of a $10 billion real-estate project is asking its condo buyers for money.

The total value of building permits rose 8.8% from the month before to a seasonally adjusted 13.57 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of $9.55 billion, Statistics Canada said.

Mortgage rates above 7% might not be enough to crack home values if owners hold the line.

The 1.5% gain over the previous month reflected a plateau in mortgage rates over the summer, but sales activity overall remained subdued.

The loan—based on potential rental income, not the borrower’s wealth—is helping real-estate investors buy and renovate homes.

Competition for buyers is heating up, which will force companies like Lennar and KB home to beef up incentives.

The highest mortgage rates in three years are putting pressure on home prices in some metro areas where the market is starting to tilt toward buyers.

The rise to 7.28% follows the bond-market rout and deals another blow to a limping housing market.

With prices at record highs and inventory locked up, house hunters are left with dwindling financing options.

title: Jobs
content:

Private companies added a net 86,000 jobs in October, ADP said. Economists polled expected 75,000 new private-sector jobs.

U.S. job openings rose in September while hiring held relatively steady, according to a report from the Labor Department’s monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey.

As women make inroads in male-dominated fields, firms look to improve jobsite culture.

In California, home to the nation’s highest gas prices, tens of thousands of Uber and Lyft drivers are joining forces.

Employers in Canada cut 68,300 jobs in September, nudging the unemployment rate up 0.1 percentage point to 6.5%.

The number of people who filed for unemployment benefits was 197,000 in the week through Oct. 3, lower than the revised 199,000 reported a week earlier, the Labor Department said.

Anemic hiring fell far short of expectations with 29,000 jobs added last month, but the unemployment rate remains near historic lows.

To justify staggering investment sums, Americans will have to spend as much of their income on this one technology as they do on food.

Unemployment stayed at 6.4% in August, even with higher interest rates and an energy crunch driven by war in the Middle East.

Private companies added a net 90,000 jobs in September, up from a revised 36,000 jobs added in August, ADP said. Economists had expected to see 68,000 new private-sector jobs added.

U.S. jobless claims fell to 197,000 in the week through Sept. 19, according to the Labor Department. Economists surveyed had expected initial unemployment claims to rise to 201,000.

Data-center spending is greater than that for canals, railroads and grid combined—creating jobs and stock-market wealth, while boosting inflation and crowding out housing.

title: Trade
content:
The widening to C$5.35 billion in September marked the the biggest surplus in over four years as exports hit a fresh record high.

Imports were higher than exports by $105 billion, down 0.7% from August, in contrast to economists’ expectations for the trade gap to widen.

The Trump administration has promised to ease tariffs on automakers that commit to more U.S. manufacturing, according to people familiar with the situation.
